screens.title: Reading Smart Contract Data from the Frontend
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to read data from a deployed smart contract directly from your frontend. Reading uses view and pure functions that do not change blockchain state, so calls are fast and free. You'll see what pieces you need — the contract address and the ABI — and how to use Ethers. js to create a contract instance with a provider to perform read-only queries. We will ground the ideas with a compact Greeter contract example that exposes a public name variable and a greet function. I'll show how to import the ABI into a React project, initialize the ethers. Contract object, and call the contract's auto-generated getter for public variables. We'll also cover one important contrast: when you need a signer versus when a provider is enough. Finally, I'll highlight common mistakes you will encounter in practice — incorrect address, outdated ABI, and network mismatch — and what simple checks you can do to confirm the data returned is valid. By the end you will be able to fetch and render a greeting message and a contract name in your dApp interface with basic error handling.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to create a contract instance in your frontend and read its state safely. First, you'll instantiate an Ethers. js contract object with the contract address and ABI and understand why both pieces are required to form the interface. Second, you'll call view and pure functions from the frontend using a provider so you can fetch data without paying gas. Third, you'll render the returned values in React state so the dApp UI updates automatically when data is loaded. Finally, you'll add basic error handling around your read calls to surface helpful messages to users when the address, ABI, or network is incorrect. Each objective is practical: you will import the ABI from your Hardhat artifacts, use a provider to initialize the contract, call the contract's getter or view function, and implement try-catch logic to handle failed calls. These skills reduce development friction and make your dApp more resilient during network changes or user disconnects.

screens.title: What view and pure functions mean
screens.narratorSegment: View and pure functions are Solidity declarations that guarantee the function will not modify blockchain state. A view function may read state variables but makes no state changes; a pure function cannot even read state and only computes values from its inputs. Because neither changes the state, calling them from your frontend does not create a transaction, does not require gas, and returns a result immediately from a node. This is why these functions are the primary mechanism for showing current contract state in your dApp. For example, if a Greeter contract exposes a public name variable, the compiler automatically generates a getter function you can call from JavaScript. A common misconception is thinking that all functions are free to call; in practice, only view and pure are read-only. If a function writes or emits events, or calls other non-view functions, it will require a transaction and a signer. The key takeaway is to design your contract A P I so data that needs to be displayed frequently is exposed through view or pure functions. That lets the frontend query the current state quickly and show users live information without asking them to sign a transaction.

keyIdea.title: Read-only = no gas
keyIdea.text: Use view and pure functions to fetch state instantly and without transactions from a provider.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › View & Pure Functions
Definition

A view function may read state but does not alter it. A pure function does not even read state and returns computed values only.

Concrete example
A public string variable such as name has an auto-generated getter you can call from JavaScript to obtain the current name.
Common mistake
Trying to call a function that changes state as if it were free will require a signer and will fail when using only a provider.
Why this matters for UIs
  • Reads are instant and cheap, so you can update UI frequently without asking the user to confirm.
  • Designate display-only getters for any state you expect the client to show often.
  • Use pure functions for deterministic calculations that depend only on inputs.
Key Takeaway

Expose read-only state via view or pure functions so the frontend can fetch live data quickly and without gas.

screens.title: Contract Address and ABI — the two essentials
screens.narratorSegment: Two specific artifacts are required to call a deployed contract from your frontend: the contract address and the ABI. The address is the unique network location returned during deployment; it tells a node which on-chain contract you mean. The ABI is a JSON array that describes the contract's public methods, events, and types so Ethers. js can encode calls and decode results. In a Hardhat project the ABI is available inside artifacts/contracts/YourContract. sol/YourContract. json after compilation and deployment. A common workflow is to copy this JSON into a src/contracts folder in your frontend and then import it. If you redeploy or change functions you must update the ABI copy in the frontend, otherwise calls can fail with errors like "not a function". Another gotcha is network specificity: the same address may not exist on another network, and deploying twice produces different addresses. So verifying the address corresponds to the network your wallet is connected to is the fastest initial sanity check when a read fails. Together the address locates the contract and the ABI describes how to talk to it; both are indispensable.

keyIdea.title: Address locates, ABI describes
keyIdea.text: The address points to the deployed contract; the ABI tells your frontend how to call its functions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Address & ABI
Contract Address

A hexadecimal identifier returned at deployment. Keep the exact address for the network where you deployed.

Quick sanity check

If a call reverts, confirm the address matches the network shown in your wallet. A wrong network is the most common cause of read failure.

ABI (Application Binary Interface)

A JSON array describing public functions and events. Hardhat writes this into artifacts after compilation.

Why update it

If you change your contract and redeploy, update the frontend ABI to match or Ethers.js won't know about new functions.

screens.title: Importing the ABI and creating the contract instance
screens.narratorSegment: In practice you'll import the artifact JSON that Hardhat produced and provide the ABI array to the Ethers. js constructor. Typically you place the Greeter. json file into src/contracts and import it. Then, once you have a provider, create the contract object by passing the contract address, the artifact's abi property, and the provider. This contract instance exposes functions corresponding to the ABI, including auto-generated getters for public variables. The provider parameter is sufficient for read-only operations. A common confusion is calling the constructor with a signer when you only need reads; a signer gives permission to send transactions but is unnecessary for view calls and can complicate testing. After creating the contract instance, you can immediately call read methods or store the instance in state so other effects can re-use it. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Import & Instantiate
Key steps
  • Copy Greeter.json into src/contracts.
  • Import the JSON and use its abi property.
  • Create new ethers.Contract(address, GreeterABI.abi, provider).
Example (visual only)
// Import artifact
import GreeterABI from './contracts/Greeter.json'

const GREETER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS = '0x...yourAddress...'

// Given a provider
const contract = new ethers.Contract(
  GREETER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS,
  GreeterABI.abi,
  provider
)

// Ready to call read-only functions
const greeting = await contract.greet()
const name = await contract.name()

screens.title: Initializing the contract in React with useEffect
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable pattern is to create the contract instance inside a React effect that runs when the provider becomes available. When your app detects a provider in the browser, instantiate a BrowserProvider and save it in state. Then use a second effect that watches the provider value; when that effect runs, create new ethers. Contract with the saved address, ABI, and provider, then store it in state. Immediately after creating the contract, call a fetch function to read initial data. This pattern ensures the contract instance is re-created when the provider changes, such as after a network switch. Also, add cleanup for wallet events so you remove event listeners and clear contract data on disconnect. A misconception is to create the contract before the provider is fully initialized; this can lead to undefined behavior. The flow below lists the concrete steps: detect provider, set provider in state, effect runs to create contract, call fetchContractData, render results. This approach also makes it easy to trigger re-fetching when the contract instance changes, for instance after a chain change. Initializing the contract in React with useEffect means create the contract instance in a useeffect that depends on provider so initialization and data fetching are synchronized.. In practical terms, when and how to create the contract instance and trigger data fetches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Init in React
Step-by-step
  1. Detect window.ethereum and create a provider object.
  2. Store provider in state so effects can react to it.
  3. In a useEffect watching provider, construct new ethers.Contract and set it into state.
  4. Call a fetch function immediately after instantiation to populate UI state.
Checklist & tips
  • Re-create contract when provider changes to handle network switches.
  • Keep fetch logic separate so you can call it on demand.
  • Clear stale data when the wallet disconnects to avoid confusing UI.

screens.title: Implementing fetchContractData to call read methods
screens.narratorSegment: The fetch function is the core of showing on-chain data in your UI. It takes a contract instance and calls its view functions asynchronously inside a try-catch block. For our Greeter example you will call the greet getter and the name getter, await their returned values, and then set component state so React re-renders the UI. Error handling is important: if the call throws, clear previous values and surface an error message explaining that either the address, ABI, or network may be incorrect. A common mistake is omitting await, which leaves a pending promise in state instead of the actual string. Another subtle point is that public state variables become auto-generated getter functions; you call them the same way you call other view functions. Keep the fetch function small, and call it when the contract instance is ready and also after any network or account changes that should refresh displayed data. The code block below shows the shape you should follow. Avoid sending transactions from this function — it is read-only only. Implementing fetchContractData to call read methods means call contract.greet and contract.name inside try-catch, update state, and clear values on error.. In practical terms, practical implementation: call greet and name getters and update component state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Small, async fetch function
keyIdea.text: Call contract.greet and contract.name inside try-catch, update state, and clear values on error.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › fetchContractData
Behavior to implement
  • Return early if contract instance is missing.
  • Wrap calls in try-catch and clear values on error.
  • Set state with the returned strings so the UI displays them.
Example implementation
const fetchContractData = async (contractInstance) => {
  if (!contractInstance) return
  try {
    const greeting = await contractInstance.greet()
    setGreetingMessage(greeting)

    const name = await contractInstance.name()
    setContractName(name)

    setError('')
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Error fetching contract data:', err)
    setError('Failed to fetch contract data. Ensure contract address and network are correct.')
    setGreetingMessage('')
    setContractName('')
  }
}

screens.title: Handling wallet events and keeping data fresh
screens.narratorSegment: A robust frontend listens for wallet events so the UI remains trustworthy when accounts or networks change. The common events are accountsChanged, chainChanged, and disconnect. When accounts change, you must update the stored account, refresh the signer if needed, and often clear or reload contract data because the visible account context changed. When the chain changes, the simplest safe action is to reload the page so provider internals reinitialize and the new network is used. On disconnect, clear account, signer, and contract-related state so the UI doesn't show stale on-chain values. Register listeners when you detect window. ethereum and remove them in cleanup to avoid memory leaks. Also surface clear messages to the user describing why the UI data disappeared. A common misconception is that event listeners are optional; ignoring them leads to confusing UX when a user switches networks in their wallet and the dApp continues to show data from a different chain. By handling these events you provide a predictable and correct interface for reading contract state. Handling wallet events and keeping data fresh means listen for wallet events and update or clear contract state so the data you show always matches the connected account and network.. In practical terms, respond to accountschanged, chainchanged, and disconnect to keep ui consistent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Wallet Events
accountsChanged

If the wallet account changes, update account state, refresh the signer, and re-fetch contract data or clear it if disconnected.

chainChanged

Network switches often require reloading provider state. A safe strategy is to reload and reinitialize the contract instance on chain changes.

disconnect

When the wallet disconnects, clear account, signer, and any fetched contract data so the UI does not display stale information.

Key Takeaway

Handle wallet events proactively so your read-only UI always reflects the correct account and network context.

screens.title: Provider vs Signer — which to use for reading?
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent point of confusion is the difference between provider and signer in Ethers. js. A provider gives your app read access to the blockchain by talking to a node. It is sufficient for all view and pure function calls because those do not change state. A signer wraps a provider and has the ability to sign transactions using the user's private key; it is required whenever you want to submit a transaction that modifies state. For read-only interactions, using a signer adds complexity without benefit and can cause unpredictable behavior if the signer isn't available. Another misconception is that using a signer is more secure for reads; in reality, reads are public and can be handled by the provider. Use a provider to build fast, gas-free UI reads, and only request a signer at the moment you need to send a transaction. This separation simplifies testing and reduces prompts to the user while keeping your UI responsive. In short: provider = reads, signer = writes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Provider vs Signer
Provider

Gives read-only access to a node. Use it for view and pure calls that do not require signing.

Best for

Fetching current state for the UI, non-sensitive queries, caching results.

Signer

Wraps a provider and can sign transactions with the user's private key. Required for state-changing operations.

Use sparingly

Only request a signer when the user intends to send a transaction to reduce prompts and simplify testing.

screens.title: Error handling and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Error handling for reads should be simple and informative. Wrap contract calls in try-catch. If a call fails, log the error for debugging and set a user-facing message explaining likely causes: incorrect contract address, outdated ABI, or the wallet connected to another network. For example, a missing function error usually means the imported ABI doesn't include the function signature, while a call revert often indicates the address points to a different contract or one deployed to another network. Always clear stale UI values when an error occurs so the interface does not display misleading information. Avoid showing raw error objects to users; instead show a friendly instruction such as: "Failed to fetch contract data. Ensure contract address and network are correct." Common failures

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to read data from a deployed smart contract directly from your frontend. Reading uses view and pure functions that do not change blockchain state, so calls are fast and free. You'll see what pieces you need — the contract address and the ABI — and how to use Ethers. js to create a contract instance with a provider to perform read-only queries. We will ground the ideas with a compact Greeter contract example that exposes a public name variable and a greet function. I'll show how to import the ABI into a React project, initialize the ethers. Contract object, and call the contract's auto-generated getter for public variables. We'll also cover one important contrast: when you need a signer versus when a provider is enough. Finally, I'll highlight common mistakes you will encounter in practice — incorrect address, outdated ABI, and network mismatch — and what simple checks you can do to confirm the data returned is valid. By the end you will be able to fetch and render a greeting message and a contract name in your dApp interface with basic error handling.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create a contract instance in your frontend and read its state safely. First, you'll instantiate an Ethers. js contract object with the contract address and ABI and understand why both pieces are required to form the interface. Second, you'll call view and pure functions from the frontend using a provider so you can fetch data without paying gas. Third, you'll render the returned values in React state so the dApp UI updates automatically when data is loaded. Finally, you'll add basic error handling around your read calls to surface helpful messages to users when the address, ABI, or network is incorrect. Each objective is practical: you will import the ABI from your Hardhat artifacts, use a provider to initialize the contract, call the contract's getter or view function, and implement try-catch logic to handle failed calls. These skills reduce development friction and make your dApp more resilient during network changes or user disconnects.

These additional objectives connect the concepts to a practical workflow you will apply immediately. You will copy the ABI from your Hardhat artifacts into your frontend project and verify the contract address you deployed. You will modify your App component to add state variables for the contract instance and for values returned from the chain, such as a greeting message and a name. You will write a function to fetch contract data asynchronously and call it when the provider or contract instance becomes available. You will test the flow by running the dApp, connecting a wallet, and confirming that the read values appear. Along the way you'll practice diagnosing three common failures: wrong contract address, outdated ABI, and network mismatch. Each diagnostic is a small test that quickly narrows the cause so you can return the dApp to a working state. These are the hands-on competencies that will make your frontend reliably reflect on-chain state.

View and pure functions are Solidity declarations that guarantee the function will not modify blockchain state. A view function may read state variables but makes no state changes; a pure function cannot even read state and only computes values from its inputs. Because neither changes the state, calling them from your frontend does not create a transaction, does not require gas, and returns a result immediately from a node. This is why these functions are the primary mechanism for showing current contract state in your dApp. For example, if a Greeter contract exposes a public name variable, the compiler automatically generates a getter function you can call from JavaScript. A common misconception is thinking that all functions are free to call; in practice, only view and pure are read-only. If a function writes or emits events, or calls other non-view functions, it will require a transaction and a signer. The key takeaway is to design your contract A P I so data that needs to be displayed frequently is exposed through view or pure functions. That lets the frontend query the current state quickly and show users live information without asking them to sign a transaction.

Two specific artifacts are required to call a deployed contract from your frontend: the contract address and the ABI. The address is the unique network location returned during deployment; it tells a node which on-chain contract you mean. The ABI is a JSON array that describes the contract's public methods, events, and types so Ethers. js can encode calls and decode results. In a Hardhat project the ABI is available inside artifacts/contracts/YourContract. sol/YourContract. json after compilation and deployment. A common workflow is to copy this JSON into a src/contracts folder in your frontend and then import it. If you redeploy or change functions you must update the ABI copy in the frontend, otherwise calls can fail with errors like "not a function". Another gotcha is network specificity: the same address may not exist on another network, and deploying twice produces different addresses. So verifying the address corresponds to the network your wallet is connected to is the fastest initial sanity check when a read fails. Together the address locates the contract and the ABI describes how to talk to it; both are indispensable.

In practice you'll import the artifact JSON that Hardhat produced and provide the ABI array to the Ethers. js constructor. Typically you place the Greeter. json file into src/contracts and import it. Then, once you have a provider, create the contract object by passing the contract address, the artifact's abi property, and the provider. This contract instance exposes functions corresponding to the ABI, including auto-generated getters for public variables. The provider parameter is sufficient for read-only operations. A common confusion is calling the constructor with a signer when you only need reads; a signer gives permission to send transactions but is unnecessary for view calls and can complicate testing. The following visual code block shows the precise shape you should use in a React component. Note that when importing the JSON you refer to its abi property, because the file also contains deployment metadata. After creating the contract instance, you can immediately call read methods or store the instance in state so other effects can re-use it. Importing the ABI and creating the contract instance means import greeter.json, use greeterabi.abi with the address and a provider to make a contract instance for reads.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A reliable pattern is to create the contract instance inside a React effect that runs when the provider becomes available. When your app detects a provider in the browser, instantiate a BrowserProvider and save it in state. Then use a second effect that watches the provider value; when that effect runs, create new ethers. Contract with the saved address, ABI, and provider, then store it in state. Immediately after creating the contract, call a fetch function to read initial data. This pattern ensures the contract instance is re-created when the provider changes, such as after a network switch. Also, add cleanup for wallet events so you remove event listeners and clear contract data on disconnect.
